News & Politics

The decision comes nearly one year after the fatal shootings of Rep. Melissa and Mark Hortman and the attacks on Sen. John Hoffman, his wife, Yvette, and their daughter, Hope.

By Jeff Day and

Paul Walsh

The Department of Justice will not seek the death penalty against Vance Boelter in the attacks on Minnesota lawmakers last summer, officials announced Monday.

The decision comes nearly one year after the June 14, 2025, shooting spree that killed state Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark. Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, and their daughter, Hope, were attacked, and Hoffman and his wife were injured.

Boelter has pleaded not guilty to the six federal charges filed against him.

The Department of Justice said it agrees with the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota that an interstate stalking conviction does not constitute eligibility for the death penalty.

U.S. Supreme Court opinions and federal case law support this position, the DOJ said.

“Bringing justice to the families and loved ones of victims of violence is the Number One priority of the Department of Justice,” an agency spokesperson said in a statement. “Prosecutors worked hard on this case to make sure [Boelter] was held accountable to the fullest extent possible.”

The first two counts against Boelter allege that he stalked the Hortmans and Hoffmans through the use of interstate facilities. In order to seek the death penalty, those charges had to rise to a crime of violence and be tied to the murder charges against Boelter in the killing of the Hortmans “through use of a firearm.”

Prosecutors had argued when charging Boelter that stalking his victims was a crime of violence. In dropping the pursuit of the death penalty, the Justice Department noted that federal courts have ruled that stalking is not always a crime of violence.

KSTP-TV was the first news outlet to report that the Justice Department was declining to seek the death penalty against Boelter.

The decision comes four months after U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett in  New York dismissed a nearly identical federal murder charge against Luigi Mangione in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. In dismissing that charge, Garnett ruled that she  did so to “foreclose the death penalty as an available punishment to be considered by the jury” as it weighs whether to convict Mangione.

To seek the death penalty, prosecutors had to show that Mangione killed Thompson while committing another “crime of violence.” Prosecutors had tied Mangione’s murder charge to his stalking charge, but Garnett wrote that stalking doesn’t fit the definition of a “crime of violence,” citing case law and legal precedents.

In Hennepin County District Court, Boelter potentially faces  life in prison for two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, four counts of first-degree attempted murder, including against Rep. Kristin Bahner, whose home he allegedly visited that night while she was out of town. He also faces one count of animal cruelty against the  the Hortmans’ dog, Gilbert, who was shot and had to be euthanized, and one count of impersonating a police officer.
